module_1_basic.title: Module 1: Basic Silver Identification
module_1_basic.description: Learn to tell solid silver from plated in 60 seconds. Perfect for estate sale floor.

lessons.title: The Two Marks That Matter Most
lessons.content:
When you pick up any silver-looking item, look for ONE of these marks:

**SOLID SILVER (WORTH $$$$):**
- `925` — 92.5% silver (most common)
- `STERLING` — American sterling
- `800` or `835` — European silver
- `Lion Passant` (walking lion) — British sterling

**NOT SOLID SILVER (WORTH $):**
- `EPNS` — Electroplated Nickel Silver (NOT silver)
- `SILVER PLATED` or `SP` — Thin coating
- `EP` — Electroplated
- `A1` — American plated

**Quick Rule:** If you see EPNS/Plated/EP/A1 — walk away. It's not solid silver.
If you see 925/Sterling/800 — it's solid silver. Check weight and condition.

**Pro Tip:** EPNS items were popular 1840-1920. Old EPNS can still be collectible ($5-50), but it's NOT solid silver.

lessons.title: The Weight Test (60 Seconds)
lessons.content:
**Why it works:** Solid silver is dense and heavy. Plated items use thin silver over light base metal.

**How to test:**
1. Pick up the item — does it feel HEAVY for its size?
2. Compare to a similar known item if possible
3. Solid silver feels noticeably heavier

**Weight Benchmarks:**
- Teaspoon: Solid = 15-20g | Plated = 8-12g
- Dinner fork: Solid = 25-35g | Plated = 15-20g
- Soup spoon: Solid = 30-40g | Plated = 18-25g

**Rule of thumb:** If it feels LIGHT, it's probably plated.
If it feels HEAVY, check for 925 mark — if present, it's solid.

**Pro Tip:** Hold a teaspoon. If you can easily flick your wrist and it bounces, it's too light = plated.

examples.verdict: Likely plated (even if marked 925, could be fake)

lessons.title: The Magnet Test (Instant)
lessons.content:
**Why it works:** Silver is NOT magnetic. If a magnet sticks, there's steel inside = plated or fake.

**How to test:**
1. Bring a magnet close to the item
2. If it ATTRACTS — NOT silver (steel core)
3. If NO attraction — could be silver OR non-magnetic base metal

**Important:** This test ONLY rules out steel. It doesn't prove silver.
- Magnet sticks = NOT silver (plated or fake)
- No stick = COULD be silver (check weight + marks)

**Pro Tip:** Most estate sale items won't have magnets, but your phone case or keys can work in a pinch. Silver won't stick.

**Common base metals:**
- Steel — magnetic (sticks to magnet) = NOT silver
- Nickel silver — non-magnetic (doesn't stick) = could be EPNS or solid
- Brass — non-magnetic (doesn't stick) = could be plated or solid

examples.verdict: Could be silver — check weight + marks

lessons.title: Wear Points (The Telltale Sign)
lessons.content:
**Why it works:** Silver plating wears off at high-contact areas, revealing the base metal underneath.

**Where to look:**
- Fork tines (tips wear fastest)
- Back of spoon bowls
- Knife blade edges
- Handle ends and tips
- Spoons where thumb rests

**What you'll see:**
- **Solid silver:** No color change at wear points. Uniform silver color everywhere
- **Plated:** Yellow/golden or copper color showing through at wear points
- **Silver wash:** Barely any silver — shows base metal immediately

**Pro Tip:** Run your fingernail along the wear point. If you feel a ridge where silver ends and base metal begins, it's plated.

**Red Flags:**
- Yellow/gold color at fork tips = PLATED
- Copper color showing through = PLATED
- Bare metal spots = PLATED or silver wash
- Uniform silver color everywhere = LIKELY SOLID

examples.item: Uniform silver, no wear color change

lessons.title: The 60-Second Estate Sale Checklist
lessons.content:
**When you pick up an item at an estate sale, do this in 60 seconds:**

**STEP 1: Look for marks (10 sec)**
- Find 925/Sterling/800 → SOLID SILVER ✓
- Find EPNS/Plated/EP/A1 → NOT SOLID ✗
- No marks? Go to Step 2

**STEP 2: Check weight (10 sec)**
- Feels heavy for size → Could be solid
- Feels light → Probably plated

**STEP 3: Check wear points (10 sec)**
- Yellow/copper showing through → PLATED ✗
- Uniform silver color → Could be solid ✓

**STEP 4: Magnet test (10 sec)**
- Magnet sticks → NOT silver ✗
- No stick → Could be silver ✓

**STEP 5: Make decision (20 sec)**
- Solid silver + good condition → BUY
- Plated but old/interesting → Maybe buy ($1-5)
- Fake or modern reproduction → Walk away

**Quick Reference Card:**
```
925 + Heavy + No wear color = SOLID SILVER ✓
EPNS/Plated + Light + Yellow wear = PLATED ✗
No marks + Heavy + Uniform color = CHECK CAREFULLY
Magnet sticks = NOT SILVER ✗
```

**Pro Tip:** At estate sales, focus on items that are HEAVY and have NO wear color showing. These are most likely solid silver.

module_2_intermediate.title: Module 2: Intermediate Silver Identification
module_2_intermediate.description: Learn to identify makers, understand British hallmarks, and spot reproductions.

lessons.title: British Hallmarks Decoded
lessons.content:
**British silver has 4+ marks that tell you everything:**

**1. Lion Passant (Walking Lion)** = 925 sterling silver
- Most recognizable British mark
- Lion shown walking, head facing left
- Used since 1300s

**2. Assay Office Mark** = Where it was tested
- London: Anchor symbol
- Birmingham: Anchor (different shield shape)
- Sheffield: Rose symbol
- Edinburgh: Castle symbol
- Glasgow: Tree with three fish

**3. Date Letter** = Year made
- Small letter in shield/oval
- Font style + shield shape = specific year
- Each office has its own alphabet cycle
- Example: Letter 'n' in square shield with pointed corners = Sheffield 1905

**4. Maker's Mark** = Who made it
- Two initials in shield/escutcheon
- Example: 'PR' = Paul Revere, 'PS' = Paul Storr
- Can be very valuable if famous maker

**5. Duty Mark (1784-1890)** = Monarch profile
- George III, William IV, or Victoria
- Shows tax paid to Crown
- Not found on items after 1890

**Valuable Periods:**
- Pre-1800 (Georgian) with assay marks
- 1837-1901 (Victorian) with maker marks
- Pieces with famous silversmith names

examples.item: Lion passant + Anchor + Letter 'A' in pointed shield
Lion passant + Rose + Letter 'n' in square shield

lessons.title: Famous American Silver Makers
lessons.content:
**These maker marks add significant value:**

**Tiffany & Co.** (1837-present)
- Mark: 'TIFFANY & CO.' with pattern number
- Value: Extremely valuable. Museum quality.
- Look for: Art Nouveau designs, high craftsmanship

**Reed & Barton** (1824-2015)
- Mark: 'RB' or 'Reed & Barton' with pattern number
- Location: Taunton, Massachusetts
- Value: Quality American silver. Sterling pieces valuable.
- Note: Bankrupt 2015, but antique pieces still collectible

**Gorham** (1831-2010)
- Mark: 'GORHAM' with Greek key symbol or pattern number
- Value: High-quality. Art Nouveau designs very collectible.
- Note: Known for ornate, decorative pieces

**International Silver Co.** (1870-1960s)
- Mark: 'IC' or 'International' with crown
- Value: Common but collectible. Quality silver plate and sterling.
- Note: Merged several companies

**Wm. Rogers & Co.** (1830-1960s)
- Mark: 'WR & Co' or 'Rogers' with pattern
- Value: Common silver plate. Some sterling pieces valuable.
- Note: Check for 925 mark to confirm sterling

**Towle Silver Co.** (1840-1970s)
- Mark: 'Towle' with pattern number
- Value: American silver plate and sterling

**Oneida Silver Co.** (1890s-present)
- Mark: 'Oneida' with pattern number
- Value: Common American silver plate

**Quick Rule:** If you see Tiffany, Gorham, or Reed & Barton with 925 mark — it's valuable solid silver. Check condition and pattern rarity.

lessons.title: Spotting Reproductions and Fakes
lessons.content:
**Modern reproductions are common. Here's how to spot them:**

**1. Too Perfect Condition**
- Antique items should show SOME wear
- Perfect condition + shiny = likely reproduction
- Exception: Items stored in boxes for decades

**2. Modern Font Styles**
- Antique items have period-appropriate stamping
- Clean, machine-made fonts on 'antique' = reproduction
- Hand-stamped marks have slight variations

**3. Wrong Hallmark Combinations**
- Lion passant + 925 mark = WRONG (lion is British, 925 is American/European)
- Check that marks match the period and region

**4. Weight Doesn't Match**
- Heavy item marked '925' but feels light = fake
- Solid silver has consistent weight for size

**5. Wear Points Don't Match Age**
- 'Antique' item with no wear = suspicious
- Real antique flatware shows wear on fork tines, spoon backs

**6. Machine-Made Uniformity**
- Real hallmarks have slight variations (hand-stamped)
- Perfectly identical marks on multiple items = machine-made reproduction

**7. Wrong Materials**
- Brass stamped with fake 925 marks
- Nickel silver (non-magnetic) can fool magnet test
- Always check weight + wear points too

**Red Flags Checklist:**
- [ ] Perfect condition with no wear?
- [ ] Modern font styles on 'antique' item?
- [ ] Hallmark combinations that don't match period?
- [ ] Weight feels wrong for size?
- [ ] Marks too perfect/identical?

**If 2+ red flags = likely reproduction. Walk away.**

examples.item: Perfect condition, modern font, no wear
Heavy item, no marks, uniform silver
examples.verdict: CHECK CAREFULLY — could be unmarked solid

examples.item: Slight variations in hallmarks, some wear

lessons.title: Old Sheffield Plate vs Electroplate
lessons.content:
**Old Sheffield Plate (OSP) was made 1740s-1840s. It's NOT electroplated.**

**How OSP was made:**
- Silver and copper sheets fused together under heat/pressure
- Invented by Thomas Boulsover (1740s)
- Replaced by electroplating ~1840

**How to identify OSP:**

**1. Copper Bleeding**
- Silver and copper fused, not plated
- At wear points, copper 'bleeds' through (reddish color)
- Different from plated (which shows brass/copper base)

**2. Bluish Cast**
- OSP has distinctive 'very faintly bluish lustre'
- Electroplate has brilliant, hard color
- OSP is harder than electroplated silver

**3. Soldered Joints**
- OSP made from pre-plated metal sheet/wire
- Look for soldered joints (hallmark of OSP)
- Electroplate constructed in base metal then plated

**4. No EP Marks**
- OSP never marked 'EP' or 'EPNS'
- If you see EP/EPNS, it's electroplated (post-1840)

**5. Age Indicators**
- OSP items pre-1840 (check for period-appropriate marks)
- Electroplate post-1840

**Value:**
- Genuine OSP pre-1800 can be VERY valuable ($100-500+)
- Collectors seek genuine OSP
- Many electroplate reproductions exist — verify carefully

**Quick Test:**
```
Copper bleeding + Bluish cast + Soldered joints = OSP ✓
EP/EPNS marks + Brilliant color + No soldering = Electroplate ✗
```

examples.verdict: Likely OSP — check for copper bleeding

examples.item: Perfect condition, no wear, EP marks

lessons.title: European Silver Marks Quick Guide
lessons.content:
**Different countries have different hallmark systems:**

**French Silver (Post-1838):**
- Minerva head (goddess in profile) = solid silver
- Numeral 1 = 950 fineness (95% silver)
- Numeral 2 = 800 fineness (80% silver)
- Maker's mark in lozenge shape with initials
- Export marks: Mercury head with number (920, 840, 750)

**German Silver:**
- Cross pattee (decorated cross) = silver hallmark
- 800 or 925 fineness marks common
- Maker's mark usually initials in shield

**Swiss Silver:**
- Maiden's head = Swiss assay mark
- 800 or 925 fineness marks

**Austria-Hungary (1867-1933):**
- Crowned Diana head within geometric frame
- Frame shape indicates fineness:
  - Concave lines = 140 per line
  - Straight lines = 150 per line
  - Convex lines = 160 per line
- Example: 5-petal flower frame = 5×160 = 800 fineness
- Hexagonal frame = 900 fine silver

**Japanese Silver (Post-1929):**
- Japan Mint assays and hallmarks
- Mark: Figure of Japanese flag (rising sun)
- Fineness marks: 800, 900, 950

**Quick Identification:**
- Minerva head = French
- Cross pattee = German
- Diana head + frame = Austria-Hungary
- Rising sun = Japanese

module_3_advanced.title: Module 3: Advanced Silver Identification
module_3_advanced.description: Master rare hallmarks, date letter decoding, and high-value identification.

lessons.title: British Date Letter System
lessons.content:
**Date letters tell you EXACTLY when a British silver piece was made.**

**How it works:**
- Each assay office has its own alphabet cycle
- Letter style (font, case, shield shape) changes each decade
- Same letter in different shields = different years

**Example: Sheffield Date Letters**
- Square shield, pointed corners, lowercase 'n' = 1905
- Oval shield, rounded corners, uppercase 'N' = 1895
- Each decade has unique shield shape + font combination

**Example: London Date Letters**
- Different shield shapes for each period
- Font styles change (serif, sans-serif, italic)
- Letter case changes (upper/lower) per decade

**How to read:**
1. Find the date letter (small, separate from other marks)
2. Note the shield shape around it
3. Note the font style (serif, italic, block)
4. Match to assay office calendar

**Valuable Periods:**
- Pre-1700 (very rare, extremely valuable)
- 1700-1800 (Georgian era, highly collectible)
- 1837-1901 (Victorian era, popular with collectors)

**Pro Tips:**
- Date letters are usually the 3rd or 4th mark
- They're smaller than other hallmarks
- Look for them on the back/underside of items
- Online databases can help identify specific years

examples.verdict: Made in early 1700s (specific year depends on shield)
Made in specific year per Birmingham calendar

lessons.title: Rare and Valuable Hallmarks
lessons.content:
**These rare marks indicate HIGH VALUE:**

**Pre-1700 British Silver:**
- Very rare, museum quality
- Often just maker's mark + leopard head (pre-Lion Passant)
- Values: $1,000-$50,000+ depending on maker and condition

**Paul de Lamerie (1689-1751):**
- Most famous English silversmith
- Mark: 'PL' monogram in shield
- Values: $5,000-$100,000+ for holloware
- Known for ornate, decorative pieces

**Paul Revere (1732-1808):**
- American colonial silversmith
- Mark: 'PR' monogram
- Values: $10,000-$500,000+ for significant pieces
- Colonial American silver is extremely collectible

**Paul Storr (1771-1844):**
- British silversmith, Victorian era
- Mark: 'PS' or full name
- Values: $500-$10,000+ depending on piece
- Known for elegant, refined designs

**Thomas Kirk (1765-1830):**
- British Georgian silversmith
- Mark: 'TK' monogram
- Values: $300-$5,000+ for quality pieces

**Georgian Period (1714-1830):**
- Highly collectible
- Look for: Lion passant + date letter + maker mark
- Values: $200-$5,000+ depending on condition and maker

**Victorian Period (1837-1901):**
- Popular with collectors
- Look for: Victoria duty mark (1784-1890)
- Values: $50-$2,000+ depending on maker and condition

**Britannia Standard (958):**
- Higher purity than sterling (95.8% vs 92.5%)
- Obligatory in Britain 1697-1720
- Optional standard thereafter
- Values: Premium over sterling due to higher purity and rarity

examples.verdict: Paul de Lamerie piece — extremely valuable

lessons.title: Weighted Silver and Advanced Fakes
lessons.content:
**Advanced fakes require careful inspection:**

**Weighted Silver:**
- Silver shell filled with lead or other heavy metal
- Designed to SIMULATE solid silver weight
- X-ray required for definitive detection
- Sound test: Hollow sound when tapped = possible weighted silver
- Temperature test: Lead core may feel different temperature

**Sterling Over Base:**
- Solid silver top over base metal bottom
- Common in bowls and large vessels
- Check INSIDE the bowl — if different mark or no mark, may be silver top only
- Value: Less than full solid silver

**Silver Wash:**
- Extremely thin silver coating (much thinner than plate)
- Wears off quickly with use
- Shows base metal at ANY wear point
- Very light weight
- Low value ($1-5)

**Base Metal with Fake Marks:**
- Brass or nickel silver stamped with fake 925 marks
- Magnet test won't catch (nickel silver is non-magnetic)
- Must check weight + wear points
- Wear points show brass/copper color

**Reproductions of Famous Patterns:**
- Modern items made to look like antique Tiffany/Gorham
- Check: Weight, mark quality, wear patterns, period accuracy
- Modern reproductions often have cleaner, sharper marks
- Antique pieces show slight variations (hand-stamped)

**Advanced Detection Checklist:**
1. Weight matches expected for size?
2. Wear points show uniform silver (not base metal)?
3. Marks are period-appropriate (font, style, combination)?
4. No hollow sound when tapped?
5. Temperature feels consistent throughout?
6. Inside shows same silver as outside?

**If 3+ checks fail = likely fake or reproduction.**

Shows base metal at slightest wear

lessons.title: Coin Silver and US Silver Coins
lessons.content:
**US silver coins are a major source of silver at estate sales:**

**Pre-1965 US Coins (90% Silver):**
- Dimes (pre-1965): 0.0723 troy oz silver each
- Quarters (pre-1965): 0.1600 troy oz silver each
- Half dollars (pre-1965): 0.3616 troy oz silver each
- Dollars (various): 0.7734 troy oz silver each

**Identification:**
- Check date — pre-1965 = silver (mostly)
- Look for mint marks (small letters near date)
- Edge should be reeded (grooved), not smooth
- Weight and size match specifications

**Morgan Dollars (1878-1921):**
- Most collectible US silver dollar
- 0.7734 troy oz silver
- Values: $20-$1,000+ depending on condition and date
- Look for: 'E PLURIBUS UNUM', liberty head design

**Barber Dimes/Quarters (1892-1916):**
- 90% silver
- Collectible, especially in good condition
- Values: $5-$100+ depending on date and condition

**Mercury Dimes (1916-1945):**
- 90% silver
- Popular with collectors
- Values: $3-$50+ depending on date and condition

**Pre-1837 'Coin Silver':**
- American standard before 1868
- Made from melted coins (90.3% silver)
- Marked 'COIN SILVER' or 'PURE COIN'
- Sometimes just '903'
- Historically significant
- Values: $20-$500+ depending on item and condition

**Quick Rule:** Any US coin before 1965 (except pennies) is likely silver. Check date first!

lessons.title: Advanced Pattern Identification
lessons.content:
**Pattern numbers help identify value and rarity:**

**How Patterns Work:**
- Each silver company created multiple patterns (designs)
- Pattern numbers help identify specific designs
- Some patterns are rarer/more valuable than others

**Reed & Barton Patterns:**
- Many sterling and silverplate patterns
- Pattern numbers on underside or back
- Pre-1920 patterns generally more valuable
- Art Nouveau/Arts & Crafts patterns highly collectible

**Tiffany Patterns:**
- Extremely valuable, especially pre-1920
- Pattern numbers help identify rarity
- Art Nouveau designs (Louis Comfort Tiffany era) most valuable
- Some patterns produced in limited quantities

**Gorham Patterns:**
- Art Nouveau (Chrysanthemum, Greek Key) highly collectible
- Arts & Crafts patterns valuable
- Pattern numbers on underside
- Pre-1920 pieces generally more valuable

**International Silver Patterns:**
- Many patterns produced
- Check for 925 mark to confirm sterling
- Some patterns rarer than others
- Pre-1940 patterns generally more collectible

**How to Research Patterns:**
1. Find pattern number on item
2. Search online: '[Maker] [Pattern Number]' 
3. Check condition, rarity, recent sales
4. Note: Pattern alone doesn't indicate silver content — always check for 925 mark

**Value Factors:**
- Pre-1920 patterns generally more valuable
- Art Nouveau/Arts & Crafts periods premium
- Complete services (12+ place settings) worth more than individual pieces
- Matching sugar/cream sets worth more than single items
- Rare patterns command premium prices

module_4_practical.title: Module 4: Estate Sale Floor Practice
module_4_practical.description: Real-world scenarios and quick decision-making for estate sales.

lessons.title: The 5-Item Estate Sale Drill
lessons.content:
**Practice this drill at every estate sale:**

**Item 1: Teaspoon in drawer**
- Check for 925 mark
- Weigh it (15-20g = solid)
- Check wear points (no yellow/copper = good)
- Decision: BUY if solid + good condition

**Item 2: Fork in silverware chest**
- Look for maker marks (Tiffany, Gorham, RB)
- Check weight (25-35g = solid)
- Inspect tines for wear color
- Decision: BUY if famous maker + solid

**Item 3: Bowl on shelf**
- Check inside AND outside for marks
- Look for 'STERLING' or '925'
- Check weight (300g+ = likely solid)
- Decision: BUY if solid + no damage

**Item 4: Tray in cabinet**
- Look for assay marks (British) or maker marks
- Check for copper bleeding (OSP?)
- Weight test (>500g = likely solid if marked)
- Decision: BUY if rare mark or OSP

**Item 5: Coin collection**
- Check dates (pre-1965 = silver)
- Look for mint marks
- Count total silver content
- Decision: BUY if pre-1965 coins in good condition

**Quick Decision Matrix:**
```
SOLID SILVER + Good condition = BUY ($$$$
SOLID SILVER + Damage/repair = CONSIDER ($$
PLATED + Old/interesting = MAYBE ($)
PLATED + Modern reproduction = WALK AWAY
FAKE/FORGERY = WALK AWAY
```

**Pro Tips:**
- Focus on HEAVY items with NO wear color showing
- Check for famous maker marks (Tiffany, Gorham, RB)
- Look for British assay marks (Lion Passant = valuable)
- Pre-1965 coins are always silver
- When in doubt, put it back and come back later

lessons.title: Common Estate Sale Silver Scenarios
lessons.content:
**Scenario 1: Drawer full of mixed flatware**
- Sort by weight (heavy = likely solid)
- Check each for 925/Sterling mark
- Separate EPNS/Plated from solid
- Count how many are solid vs plated
- Decision: Buy lot if 50%+ solid silver

**Scenario 2: Silverware service for 12**
- Check if complete (forks, spoons, knives)
- Look for pattern number
- Verify all pieces are solid (925 mark on each)
- Check for missing pieces
- Decision: Complete service worth 2-3x individual pieces

**Scenario 3: Bowl with no marks**
- Weight test (heavy = could be solid)
- Check wear points (uniform silver = good sign)
- Magnet test (no stick = could be silver)
- Check inside for different marks
- Decision: If heavy + uniform + no magnet = likely solid, buy

**Scenario 4: Candlesticks (single vs pair)**
- PAIRS are essential for value
- Single candlestick = low value ($5-20)
- Pair of solid silver = valuable ($100-500+)
- Check both for matching marks
- Decision: Only buy pairs of solid silver

**Scenario 5: Jewelry box with mixed items**
- Check each for 925 mark
- Weight test (heavy = likely solid)
- Look for maker marks
- Separate plated from solid
- Decision: Buy lot if 30%+ solid silver pieces

**Scenario 6: Coin collection in album**
- Check dates (pre-1965 = silver)
- Count total silver content
- Note rare dates/mint marks
- Decision: Buy if mostly pre-1965 coins

**Scenario 7: Ornate decorative piece**
- Check for British assay marks (Lion Passant)
- Look for maker marks
- Weight test
- Check condition (damage reduces value significantly)
- Decision: British sterling with assay marks = valuable

**Golden Rules:**
1. Heavy + No wear color + 925 mark = SOLID SILVER
2. Pairs > Singles (candlesticks, etc.)
3. Complete services > Individual pieces
4. Pre-1965 coins = always silver
5. When in doubt, put it back
